title: A General Factor With No General Ability
scopeNote: This keeps one of the generating models from the original, the sampling account, and runs it live against a fitted single factor. The side-by-side comparison with common-factor and mutualism models, and the hierarchical and bifactor solutions, stay in the longer version. One model is enough to make the point, which is that a positive manifold does not choose between models.
summary: Six tests, fifteen hundred small independent processes, and no general ability anywhere in the model. Every correlation comes out positive and a single general factor reproduces the whole matrix to within a couple of hundredths.
learningObjectives: State what the positive manifold is.
Explain why a positive manifold does not establish that a general ability exists.
Explain how overlapping sets of small processes produce positive correlations.
Distinguish a factor that fits well from a factor that corresponds to something.
Say what kind of evidence would be needed to choose between accounts of the manifold.
Recognise that this argument does not establish the sampling account either.
interactionTypes: a judgement about what the positive manifold establishes
a live control over how much the tests draw on the same pool of processes
a correlation matrix recomputed from the model on every change
a single general factor fitted on request, with its largest residual shown
a zero-overlap setting where the manifold disappears entirely
privacy: Nothing is collected, stored or transmitted. No test is administered and nothing is inferred about the learner.
accessibilityNotes: Keyboard operable throughout, with overlap on a native range input reporting its value in text. The correlation matrix and the fitted loadings are real tables with row and column headers, so every number is reachable without a figure, and the matrix caption states in words whether all the correlations are positive and what the smallest is. A live sentence restates the current setting and its consequence in plain language. Nothing is timed and there is no motion.
dataStatus: Six generically described tests and a model of fifteen hundred independent processes. No published test is named or reproduced, no person is measured, and every correlation shown is computed from the model rather than observed.
simulationNotes: The model is Thomson's sampling account. Each test draws on a share of a pool of independent processes, and the correlation between two tests is the overlap between the sets they draw on divided by the geometric mean of their sizes, which is the correlation between two sums of shared unit-variance independent terms. Nothing in that expression is a general ability, and every off-diagonal entry is positive whenever the sets overlap at all. A single common factor is then fitted by alternating least squares on the off-diagonal entries, which is the classic minimum residual one-factor solution, and the largest absolute residual is displayed. Across the whole range of the control that residual stays below 0.023, which is the activity's claim and is verified at every setting in the test suite. Which processes each test uses is drawn once at load from seed 1947 and never redrawn; the control changes only how many each test uses, so raising it adds processes rather than swapping them and the learner watches the effect of overlap rather than sampling noise. The seed was chosen, among those producing the intended structure, for keeping the residual small at every setting rather than only at the default. Simplifications: real cognitive processes are not fifteen hundred independent things, real tests do not sample them at random, and real correlation matrices are not this tidy. The argument is also deliberately one-directional and the caution says so: showing that a sampling model produces a manifold does not show that a general ability does not exist, and does not establish the sampling account.
readmeTopic: why every cognitive test correlating with every other proves less than it seems
